title: Commands in order
content:
01. Commands in order

**You need:** Paper; Scratch or Course C are optional.

**Goal:** Create a route that another person can follow.

**Predict:** What happens if you swap the turn and the step forward?

1. Draw a 5-by-5 grid. Start at (1, 1), facing right. Finish at (4, 3). The vertical coordinate increases upwards.
2. Use the commands “move forward one square” and “turn left in place”. Write a route to the finish.
3. Move a counter using your commands. Then give the written route to a friend without showing your example.

With a robot: divide the route into short segments. Adjust the distance to the wheels and surface.

**Check yourself:** The counter reached (4, 3). You explained what each command means.

**Common mistake:** “Turn here” is unclear to the person following your instructions. Specify the direction of the turn.

More resources: [Code.org: Course C](https://studio.code.org/ru/courses/coursec-2025/units/1), [Scratch: first project](https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor/?tutorial=getStarted)

title: A strong model
content:
02. A strong model

**You need:** Paper and LEGO building instructions; you will need a kit later.

**Goal:** Explain why the pieces stay together.

**Predict:** Which part of a model might tilt if it is attached on only one side?

1. Open the LEGO instructions and find Driving Base. Look at the first steps and the finished model.
2. Draw the two sides of your frame. Mark the joints and the points where the motors attach.
3. Add a second support where a part could turn or wobble. Explain your decision.

With a kit: build the frame. An adult can help check the connections without bending the pieces forcefully.

**Check yourself:** Your drawing shows what is connected and where the extra support is.

**Common mistake:** A nice drawing does not prove strength. Test strength on the built model.

More resources: [LEGO: building instructions](https://education.lego.com/en-us/product-resources/spike-prime/downloads/building-instructions/)

title: Motion and measurement
content:
03. Motion and measurement

**You need:** A ruler and paper; the SPIKE App is optional.

**Goal:** Tell the difference between distance, a wheel rotation, and the robot’s turning angle.

**Predict:** If a motor turns 360 degrees, does the robot necessarily turn a full circle?

1. Draw a wheel and a robot viewed from above. Label “wheel rotation” and “body turn” separately.
2. Prepare a table with three rows: command, centimetres travelled, and deviation from the target. Leave the results blank for now.
3. Draw the robot body turning 90 degrees. Explain why this is different from a command to “turn the motor 90 degrees”.

With a robot: after checking the ports, repeat one short drive three times from the same starting point. Measure the result and change only one parameter at a time.

**Check yourself:** You did not equate motor degrees with the body’s turning angle or invent measurements.

**Common mistake:** One successful attempt does not establish repeatability.

More resources: [LEGO SPIKE App: editor](https://spike.legoeducation.com/prime/lobby/), [LEGO: Driving Around](https://education.lego.com/en-us/lessons/prime-competition-ready/training-camp-1-driving-around/)

title: Choose a useful attachment
content:
04. Choose a useful attachment

**You need:** Paper and a LEGO model catalogue.

**Goal:** Choose a mechanism for the task rather than for its appearance.

**Predict:** Do you need a separate motor to push a light object forward?

1. Task: move a small, light box across a table. Draw a simple pusher and a gripper that opens.
2. Mark what moves with the robot body and what needs its own drive.
3. Choose one option. Draw how it attaches to the frame and how it can be removed. Optional: draw a pair of meshed gears and arrows showing their rotation.

With a kit: an adult can help build the attachment. Test it slowly and keep fingers away from moving parts.

**Check yourself:** You explained your choice, attachment method, and the difference between passive and motorised attachments.

**Common mistake:** Do not add a motor if moving the robot body already does the job.

More resources: [LEGO: building instructions](https://education.lego.com/en-us/product-resources/spike-prime/downloads/building-instructions/)

title: Repeat without a long list
content:
05. Repeat without a long list

**You need:** Paper; Scratch or Course C are optional.

**Goal:** Replace repeated commands with one loop.

**Predict:** How many steps will you take if you repeat two forward steps three times?

1. Write six identical forward steps. Next to them, rewrite them as “repeat three times: two steps forward”.
2. Follow both versions with a counter and compare the final squares.
3. In Scratch, assemble: green flag, repeat three times, with “move 20 steps” inside. Put the character at the same starting point before every run.

With a robot: test one segment of the route first, then repeat it. Make sure the robot stops at the end.

**Check yourself:** You got six steps on paper and explained which commands belong inside the loop.

**Common mistake:** A command after the loop runs once; a command inside runs on every repetition.

More resources: [Code.org: Course C](https://studio.code.org/ru/courses/coursec-2025/units/1), [Scratch: first project](https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor/?tutorial=getStarted)

title: If an obstacle is nearby
content:
06. If an obstacle is nearby

**You need:** Paper; Course D or the SPIKE App are optional.

**Goal:** Choose an action based on a condition and plan how to stop.

**Predict:** Which branch does “if distance is less than 10” choose when the value is exactly 10?

1. Write this rule: if distance is less than 10 cm, stop; otherwise, move.
2. Test the example values 7, 10, and 14 cm. Write down the branch chosen for each.
3. Add a second signal: if the stop button is pressed OR an object is closer than 10 cm, stop. Explain the difference between OR and AND.

With a robot: distance sensor F is an example for the course; check the actual port. Check the condition in a loop and add a time limit. The teacher selects a safe threshold.

**Check yourself:** The example rule selects stop for 7 and move for 10 and 14.

**Common mistake:** Checking once before moving will not detect an object that appears later.

More resources: [Code.org: Course D](https://studio.code.org/courses/coursed-2025/units/1), [LEGO SPIKE App: editor](https://spike.legoeducation.com/prime/lobby/), [LEGO: Playing with Objects](https://education.lego.com/en-us/lessons/prime-competition-ready/training-camp-2-playing-with-objects/)

title: A counter in Scratch
content:
07. A counter in Scratch

**You need:** Scratch; use paper if you do not have a computer.

**Goal:** Store a number in a variable and change it.

**Predict:** Start at 0 and add 1 three times. What is the result?

1. In Scratch, open Variables and create a variable called “counter”.
2. Assemble: green flag; set counter to 0; repeat three times; inside the loop, change counter by 1.
3. Run twice. Explain why you set the counter to 0 at the start. On paper, write the values after each repetition.

In SPIKE, a similar counter can count program actions. Whether a real mission succeeds must be tested separately.

**Check yourself:** After each new run, the counter equals 3. On paper the values are 0, 1, 2, 3.

**Common mistake:** A call counter does not prove that a robot actually completed a mission.

More resources: [Scratch: first project](https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor/?tutorial=getStarted)

title: Your own block: a short command
content:
08. Your own block: a short command

**You need:** Scratch; the SPIKE App is optional.

**Goal:** Distinguish a block’s definition from a call to that block.

**Predict:** Does creating a block make the character start moving immediately?

1. In Scratch, open My Blocks and create “short step”. Under its definition, add “move 20 steps”.
2. Under the green flag, add two calls to “short step”. Set the same starting point before running.
3. Run it. Explain to a friend where the block’s action is defined and where you ask it to perform that action.

In SPIKE, begin with your own short movement block. Before a long route, test each block separately on the model.

**Check yourself:** Two calls produce 40 screen steps. You can identify the definition and the calls separately.

**Common mistake:** Defining a block does not run it by itself.

More resources: [Scratch: first project](https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor/?tutorial=getStarted), [LEGO SPIKE App: editor](https://spike.legoeducation.com/prime/lobby/), [LEGO: My Code, Our Program](https://education.lego.com/en-us/lessons/prime-competition-ready/my-code-our-program/)

title: Find the first error
content:
09. Find the first error

**You need:** Paper; Code.org or Scratch are optional.

**Goal:** Find where the result first differs from the plan.

**Predict:** What should you check first: every command at once, or the first incorrect position?

1. Draw a 5-by-5 grid. Start at (1, 1), facing right. Target: (3, 2). Code: forward, forward, turn right, forward.
2. Follow the code with a counter. Record the position and direction after every command.
3. Change one command. Repeat from the same start and explain why that specific change helps.

With a robot: check the algorithm, ports, and build separately. The same failure may have different causes.

**Check yourself:** Replacing “turn right” with “turn left” gets the counter to (3, 2).

**Common mistake:** If you change speed, ports, and route at the same time, it is hard to tell what caused an improvement.

More resources: [Code.org: Course C](https://studio.code.org/ru/courses/coursec-2025/units/1), [Scratch: first project](https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor/?tutorial=getStarted)

title: A light surface and a line
content:
10. A light surface and a line

**You need:** Paper; the SPIKE App is optional.

**Goal:** Understand a threshold and repeated sensor checks.

**Predict:** Example readings are 20 for dark and 80 for light. What number is halfway between them?

1. These are invented numbers for this exercise. Calculate the midpoint: (20 + 80) / 2. Write the threshold 50.
2. Stopping on a line: if reflected light is below 50, stop. Work through the values 35, 50, and 65.
3. For following the edge of a line, devise two branches: dark means a small correction in one direction; light means a correction in the other. Check the signal again and again.

With a robot: measure your own surfaces and choose a threshold. Check reflected-light mode, sensor height, and the correction direction. Colour sensor B is only the course’s example layout.

**Check yourself:** You can distinguish stopping on a line from following its edge.

**Common mistake:** The number 50 will not automatically work on every field. Colour mode and reflected-light mode provide different data.

More resources: [LEGO SPIKE App: editor](https://spike.legoeducation.com/prime/lobby/), [LEGO: Reacting to Lines](https://education.lego.com/en-us/lessons/prime-competition-ready/training-camp-3-react-to-lines/)

title: A mission and repeatability
content:
11. A mission and repeatability

**You need:** Paper; SPIKE and a kit will be needed later.

**Goal:** Design a testable mission and consistent starting conditions.

**Predict:** If the start is slightly different every time, can you compare two programs fairly?

1. Invent a practice mission: move a counter to a small box and return it to the start. This is a Tagylym practice task.
2. Draw the starting line and direction. Write down what counts as success and what counts as an error.
3. Prepare five blank rows for attempts: result, cause of an error, and one next change. On paper, move the box and reconsider the route.

With a robot: fill in the rows only after real runs. Compare like-for-like conditions and check the return and stop separately.

**Check yourself:** You have a success criterion, a start diagram, and a test plan. There are no invented wins or points.

**Common mistake:** A mission plan is not a test result. Use the current official documents for the specific FLL/WRO tournament for its rules.

More resources: [LEGO SPIKE App: editor](https://spike.legoeducation.com/prime/lobby/), [LEGO: Playing with Objects](https://education.lego.com/en-us/lessons/prime-competition-ready/training-camp-2-playing-with-objects/)

title: Show and explain your project
content:
12. Show and explain your project

**You need:** Paper; Scratch is optional.

**Goal:** Show the idea, the design, and what has actually been tested.

**Predict:** What questions could help you learn whether your idea is useful to someone else?

1. Choose a simple problem: deliver a small object or warn about an obstacle. Draw three frames: problem, solution, and test.
2. Show the sequence of actions on paper or in Scratch. Ask a friend to explain it back in their own words.
3. In one minute, explain what the model does, what has been tested, and what still needs testing on the robot. Record one piece of advice and your next change.

With a robot: add a photo of your model and real observations. Before a practice tournament, check the tasks against your teacher’s rules.

**Check yourself:** Your friend understood the idea. You can distinguish the screen example from a test of a real model.

**Common mistake:** An idea cannot be called reliable just because the picture looks good.

More resources: [Scratch: first project](https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor/?tutorial=getStarted)
